NYC Civilian Complaint Records

Exploratory Analysis and Data Quality Assessment

Authors: Faisal Hossain and Jason Wilson
Original context: CIS 9650 final project

This project examines patterns and data quality in a sample of 10,000 NYC Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) allegation records.

The analysis demonstrates API retrieval, data preparation, aggregation, and visualization using Python. It also examines how missing information and changes in data collection affect interpretation of the data.

An allegation is a recorded claim. A complaint can contain multiple allegations, and investigation findings and disciplinary outcomes describe different stages of the review process. Findings do not establish the prevalence of police misconduct, explain differences between demographic groups, or attribute motives to the individuals involved.

Source: NYC Open Data — CCRB Allegations Against Police Officers

API Setup

First, we installed and imported dependencies. This notebook retrieves public CCRB records through the Socrata API. An optional application token can be supplied through the SOCRATA_APP_TOKEN environment variable. Credentials are not stored in the notebook.

200

200 items at once should be good enough. We are going to create a loop that adds 200 items at a time to a list until the list is 10,000 items.

View Python code
#Initializing empty list
data_list = []

#Setting higher limit and offset value
limit = 200
offset = 0

#Set up while loop that will run until data_list has 10000 rows
while len(data_list) < 10000:
  response = client.get('6xgr-kwjq', limit = limit, offset=offset)
  #Add response from current response to data_list
  data_list += response
  #Check length of data_list
  print(len(data_list))
  #Increment offset by limit
  offset += limit

value_counts has shown some interesting findings.

  • The dates are all the same, so this column can be dropped.

  • Complaint ID appears to have the year as the first four digits of the ID. We can derive a year column from this column

  • Age range is expressed as a string, which could work in this case, but could be expressed more cleanly.

  • Race and Ethnicity columns overlap, but Ethnicity column is much more complicated and contains some typos. We need to decide how to handle this.

Dropping Columns

Some columns are not useful for this analysis.

  • as_of_date only has one unique date, presumably the date when this dataset was last updated

  • officer_rank_abbreviation_at_incident is redundant

  • complaint_id and allegation_record_identity are just identifiers and may or may not be useful later. We will leave them for now.

df = df.drop('officer_rank_abbreviation_at_incident',axis=1)

We noticed a few columns that may need to be fixed

  • officer_tax_id should be str (because it doesn't represent a mathematical number, it is only an identifier)

  • days_on_force should be int

  • nypd_allegation_disposition should be str

  • victim_ethnicity should be str

Also we noticed this later, but we realized by converting columns to str before filling null values, we are adding 'nan' as a string to the DataFrame. We will need to fill these before changing the data type.

View Python code

df['officer_tax_id'] = df['officer_tax_id'].astype('str')
df['days_on_force'] = df['days_on_force'].astype('Int64')

df['victim_ethnicity'] = df['victim_ethnicity'].fillna('Unknown')
df['victim_ethnicity'] = df['victim_ethnicity'].astype('str')

The following dictionary groups outcome labels into broader categories for visualization. The mapping documents which original labels are included in each category.

View Python code
#Defining categories of outcomes
outcome_categories = {
    'Major Violation': ['Substantiated (Charges)','Substantiated (Command Discipline B)',
                        'Miscellaneous - Subject Terminated','Command Discipline - B',
                        'APU Guilty','APU Command Discipline B'],
    'Violation': ['Substantiated (Formalized Training)', 'Substantiated (Command Discipline A)',
                  'Substantiated (Command Discipline)','Substantiated (Instructions)',
                  'Substantiated (Command Lvl Instructions)','Substantiated (No Recommendations)',
                  'Command Discipline - A','Instructions','Formalized Training','APU Command Discipline A',
                  'Plead Guilty - DCT','Charges and Specifications - Guilty',
                  'APU Closed: Retained, with discipline','APU Closed: Previously adjudicated, with discipline',
                  'APU Formalized Training','Negttn-Nolo contendre','Negttn-Guilty','APU Command Discipline',
                  'Substantiated'],
    'Absent Victim/Complainant': ['Complainant Uncooperative','Complainant Unavailable',
                                  'Alleged Victim Uncooperative','Witness Uncooperative',
                                  'Alleged Victim Unavailable','Witness Unavailable','Victim Unidentified'],
    'Statute of Limitations Expired': ['No Disciplinary Action-SOL','APU Closed: SOL Expired prior to APU'],
    'Officer Retired/Resigned': ['APU MOS Retired','APU Closed: MOS Resigned','Resigned',
                                 'Miscellaneous - Subject Retired','Miscellaneous - Subject Resigned',
                                 'APU Closed: MOS Retired'],
    'Dismissed/Withdrawn': ['Complaint Withdrawn','APU Dismissed','Charge Dismissed - DCT',
                            'APU Closed: Dismissed by APU','ADR-Complaint Withdrawn'],
    'Undetermined': ['Officer(s) Unidentified', 'Unable to Determine',
                     'SRAD Closure','OMB PEG Directive Closure',
                     'Miscellaneous','APU Closed: Charges not served',
                     'APU Closed: Other'],
    'Allegations Not Proven': ['Unsubstantiated','Exonerated','Unfounded','Within NYPD Guidelines',
                               'No Disciplinary Action-DUP','APU Not guilty','Not Guilty - DCT',
                               'APU Closed: Retained, without discipline','Not Guilty - OATH',
                               'APU Closed: Previously adjudicated, discipline not reported'],
    'Pending': ['Closed - Pending Litigation','APU - Decision Pending','Filed','DAO case','Board Review']
}

#Assign key where value exists in corresponding list
outcome_columns = ['ccrb_allegation_disposition', 'nypd_allegation_disposition', 'investigator_recommendation']
for column in outcome_columns:
    for i in range(len(df)):
        cell = df.loc[i, column]
        for key, value in outcome_categories.items():
            if cell is None:
              df.loc[i, column] = 'Undetermined'
            elif cell in value:
              df.loc[i, column] = key


#Check assignment
print(df[outcome_columns].value_counts())

for i in range(len(df)):

              df.loc[i,'allegation'] = key

Officer Tenure Distribution

days_on_force.hist(bins=20)

The tenure field contains negative values. The following summary checks their range before determining how to handle them in the analysis.

View Python code
days_on_force.describe()
days_on_force
count 9501.000000
mean 1968.311757

The minimum recorded tenure is negative, which is not meaningful as time on the force. Records with negative tenure are excluded from the tenure analysis.

View Python code
days_on_force = days_on_force[days_on_force >= 0]
days_on_force.hist(bins=50)
plt.title('Distribution by Officer Tenure')
plt.xlabel('Days on Force')
plt.ylabel('Count of Allegations')

A large concentration of records has zero tenure. The following count checks how many records have this value. Zero tenure alone cannot indicate the allegation occurred on an officer’s first day.

View Python code
days_on_force[days_on_force == 0].count()
np.int64(3411)

Zero tenure appears in 3,411 records. Because the meaning of these values is unclear, the following histogram includes only records with positive recorded tenure.

View Python code
days_on_force = days_on_force[days_on_force > 0].dropna()
days_on_force.hist(bins=50)
plt.title('Distribution by Officer Tenure')
plt.xlabel('Days on Force')
plt.ylabel('Count of Allegations')

Allegations are concentrated at lower tenure values. Assessing whether less experienced officers receive allegations at higher rates would require comparison with NYPD staffing data by tenure.

Interpreting the Outcomes

  • In our simplified classification, most NYPD disposition values fall into “Undetermined,” which includes missing values as well as some recorded administrative outcomes. The outcomes do not map directly to each other in some cases, so this categorization was based on the best available information on these definitions.

  • Investigator recommendations contain few values in our “Major Violation” category compared with CCRB dispositions. Because this distinction comes from our simplified classification of the original labels, it should not be interpreted as a measure of severity.

  • The difficulty of aligning outcome labels, together with missing NYPD disposition values, suggests that clearer definitions and more consistent reporting of outcome availability would improve comparisons across investigators, CCRB, and NYPD. These differences currently make direct comparisons difficult.

Group sizes and missing race information should also be considered when comparing percentages.

  • “Racial Bias” accounts for less than 1% of allegation records within every race group. A follow-up study could examine whether bias-related concerns also appear in cases classified under other allegation categories.

  • “Other Bias” also represents a small percentage of records. In our classification, it includes allegations concerning religion, language interpretation, and disability. Reviewing the original allegation labels could help clarify the patterns within this category.

Report Summary

Key Findings

  • Most records fall into our simplified “Allegations Not Proven” or “Absent Victim/Complainant” categories. Approximately 94% of NYPD disposition values are classified as “Undetermined,” making it difficult to compare outcomes across investigators, CCRB, and NYPD or determine disciplinary consequences from this sample.

  • Police Officers account for the largest share of allegation records with a known officer rank. Allegations involving higher-ranked officers are less frequent. A follow-up study using NYPD staffing and hiring data could examine whether allegation spikes coincide with increased hiring.

  • Similarly, it would be helpful to understand how data collection and reporting procedures have changed over time. Without this, it can be difficult to assess whether increases in allegations correspond to an actual increase in police misconduct or simply greater availability of data regarding these incidents.

  • Among records with a known legacy race value, Black civilians account for the largest share of allegation records. This difference warrants further investigation using population and police-contact data. Missing race values and changes in race/ethnicity collection categories limit comparisons across groups and over time.

Implications for Stakeholders

  • The high proportion of “Undetermined” NYPD dispositions limits the ability of citizens, government officials, and the NYPD to assess how allegations were resolved. More complete outcome reporting, together with clearer explanations of missing values, would improve transparency and support oversight.

  • Changes in average tenure among officers associated with allegations warrant further investigation. Combining these records with NYPD staffing, hiring, and training data could help assess whether allegation rates vary with experience and inform reviews of training and hiring practices.

  • Missing values and differences in reporting categories make the data harder for citizens, lawmakers, and the NYPD to interpret. Consistent definitions, documented changes to data collection, and clearer reporting of unavailable values would strengthen the usefulness of CCRB’s public data.
